summary:
BlindSpot is a health monitor for astronauts that does not take their word for how they feel. Sleep research shows that tired people perform badly and still rate themselves as fine, and on the way to Mars a message to Earth and the reply can take about 44 minutes.

So before each check, the astronaut guesses how well they will do. Then the laptop tests them on reaction time, near vision, hand control, pulse and balance, with no extra hardware. We compare the guess with the result and call the difference the Insight Gap. A big gap on a bad day is the dangerous case, so it raises its own alarm.

Each body system then shows GO, WATCH or NO-GO based on written rules, and the app tells the astronaut what to do without waiting for Earth. Signal delay comes from NASA's JPL Horizons data and solar storms from NASA's DONKI records. Radiation dose and cabin carbon dioxide are checked against NASA limits. It is a research prototype, not a medical device.
details:
BlindSpot is a website that runs on a laptop or a phone. Before each check, the astronaut moves a slider to guess how well they will do. Then the laptop tests them, and the app shows the difference between the guess and the result. We call that difference the Insight Gap.

There are six checks: a reaction test built to the PVT-B method, near vision with an Amsler grid, a pointing test for hand control, pulse (by tapping along or with the camera on the face or palm), five timed sit-to-stands for balance under gravity, and typed readings such as sleep, temperature, blood pressure and cabin carbon dioxide. After three readings, each result is compared with the astronaut's own normal. Written rules then give each body system a GO, WATCH or NO-GO and say what to do. The app also shows how long a reply from Earth would take today. If someone scores well below their normal, the screen switches to a focus mode with one instruction.

Sleep research shows that tired people perform badly and still rate themselves as fine, so a monitor that only asks "how do you feel?" misses the problem. BlindSpot is meant to catch the moment when an astronaut is impaired and does not know it, and to tell them what to do when a message to Earth and the reply can take up to 44 minutes.

We built it with JavaScript, React and Vite, using Meta's Astryx design system for the interface and Google's MediaPipe hand model to find the palm. The NASA data comes from JPL Horizons (Earth to Mars and Moon distance, 2023 to 2040) and DONKI (494 solar particle records). It is hosted on GitHub Pages and needs only a laptop with a webcam. We used AI coding tools to help write the code and text.

Most health tools measure the body. BlindSpot also measures how well the astronaut knows their own state, and treats a confident wrong answer as the most dangerous result. It also includes a 180-day mission replay, with a simulated crew member flown through NASA's real signal-delay and solar storm records.

Only three of the limits are NASA's (600 mSv, 3 mmHg and 2.5 mmHg); we set the rest ourselves and the app says so on every rule. Readings stay in the browser, and camera frames are never saved or sent. The balance test only applies under gravity. Every status is shown as a word, not just a colour. It is a research prototype, not a medical device, and it has not been validated in flight.
